---
fixture: n-tihonov-reordered
synthesised: true
---
MOSCOW,
February 22, 1892.


... You are mistaken in thinking you were drunk at Shtcheglov’s name-day
party — you had had a drop, that was all. You danced when they all danced,
and your jigitivka on the cabman’s box excited nothing but general delight.
I don’t remember your criticism, so it was most likely far from severe. What
I do remember is that Vvedensky and I, for some reason, roared with laughter
as we listened to you.

Do you want my biography? Here it is. I was born in Taganrog in 1860, and
finished the course at Taganrog high school in 1879, which is also the year
I began writing. In 1884 I took my degree in medicine at the
University of Moscow. I gained the Pushkin prize in 1888. In 1890 I made a journey to
Sahalin across Siberia and back by sea, and in 1891 a tour in Europe, where
I drank excellent wine and ate oysters. In 1892 I took part in an orgy in
the company of V. A. Tihonov at a name-day party. The published collections
of my works are “Motley Tales,” “In the Twilight,” “Stories,”
“Surly People,” and a novel, “The Duel.” I have sinned in the dramatic line too,
though with moderation. I have been translated into all the languages with
the exception of the foreign ones, though the Germans got to me long ago.
The Czechs and the Serbs approve of me also, and the French are not
indifferent. The mysteries of love I fathomed at the age of thirteen. I am
on the best of terms with my colleagues, doctors and literary men alike. I
am a bachelor. I should like to receive a pension. I practice medicine, and
so much so that sometimes in the summer I perform post-mortems, though I
have not done so for two or three years. Of authors my favourite is Tolstoy,
of doctors Zaharin.

All that is nonsense though. Write what you like. If you haven’t facts make
up with lyricism.
